VIDEO.title: The Hidden Threat Inside the Church
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: Whoever therefore will humble himself as this child…
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 18:1-14. The disciples ask who is greatest in the kingdom of heaven. Jesus sets a child before them: unless they are converted and become like children they will never enter it, and whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest. Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble would be better drowned with a millstone around his neck. Cut off the hand or foot, tear out the eye, that causes you to stumble. Do not despise the little ones; the Father seeks the one straying sheep.

This is the fourth of Jesus' five discourses in Matthew, the discourse on church community, after the Sermon on the Mount (5-7), the mission discourse (10) and the parables (13). Five discourses recall the five books of Torah.

The video traces the disciples' argument back to the temple tax (17:24-27): they heard 'the sons are exempt' as a promise of status, not of God's provision. Mark and Luke tell of the argument (Mark 9:33-34; Luke 9:46).

Becoming like a child is about being lowly and dependent, not uneducated or naive. Jesus holds people accountable for the faith of others, and the hyperbole of cutting off a hand works like a fence around the Torah that drives the problem back to the heart. The one-sheep picture recalls Ezekiel 34, where God judges shepherds who fed themselves and scattered the flock.
The lesson: to be a part of God's community, Jesus' disciples must get rid of all forms of pride and self-seeking, and be tremendously concerned with depending on God and taking care of His sheep.
QUOTES: In order to be a part of God's community, Jesus' disciples must get rid of all forms of pride and self-seeking.
Pride is the great temptation that must be cut off.
When a person becomes prideful, the quickest, most obvious way to identify this is in their lack of concern for those around them.
It's not about being uneducated or naive. It's about being lowly and humble.

method.p: The teacher reads 18:1-14 as one answer to one bad question. The child, the millstone, the cut-off hand and the lost sheep all respond to 'Who then is greatest?' Read them together and the problem comes into focus: pride.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Truly I say to you, unless you are converted and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
See that you do not despise one of these little ones, for I say to you that their angels in heaven continually see the face of My Father who is in heaven.
In this way, it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones perish.

left.text: At that time the disciples came to Jesus and said, “Who then is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?”

right.text: And when Peter said, “From strangers,” Jesus said to him, “Then the sons are exempt.

lines.text: The video thinks the argument grew out of the temple-tax teaching. Jesus meant that God provides for His children; they heard that they now had great status as sons of the King.
How wrong is that question? Jesus immediately recognized what it revealed: pride.

GREATEST.title: A real child in the middle

src.text: And He called a child to Himself and set him before them, and said, “Truly I say to you, unless you are converted and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever therefore will humble himself as this child, he is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.

lines.text: Like a good Jewish rabbi, Jesus points to a real child. It is not about being uneducated or naive, but lowly and humble, relying on the heavenly Father for all things as little children rely on their parents.
Remember the Beatitudes: 'Blessed are the lowly, for they shall inherit the earth' (Matthew 5:5).

left.text: But they kept silent, for on the way they had discussed with one another which of them was the greatest.

right.text: and said to them, “Whoever receives this child in My name receives Me, and whoever receives Me receives Him who sent Me; for the one who is least among all of you, this is the one who is great.”

lines.text: For more details on the argument, the video points to Mark 9:33-34 and Luke 9:46.
Mark sets the scene in a house in Capernaum (Mark 9:33).

Matthew gathers Jesus' teaching into five discourses: the Sermon on the Mount (5-7), mission (10), parables (13), church community (18), and a fifth still to come. Every good Jew would have recognized the parallel with the five books of Torah.
Each discourse closes with the same formula: 'when Jesus had finished these words' (7:28; 19:1; 26:1), 'finished giving instructions' (11:1), 'finished these parables' (13:53).

src.text: but whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it is better for him that a heavy millstone be hung around his neck, and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea.

lines.text: Jesus holds people accountable for the faith of others. If a pastor's moral failing causes people to fall away, whose fault is that? We cannot answer properly without wrestling with this verse.
The Greek says a donkey's millstone (mylos onikos), the large upper stone turned by an animal, not a small hand mill.

left.text: Do not, many of you, become teachers, my brothers, knowing that we will receive a stricter judgment.

right.text: and not a new convert, so that he will not become conceited and fall into the condemnation of the devil.

lines.text: If you want to be a pastor but lack strong character and self-control, sit down and stay away from leadership until you grow up, however articulate or gifted you are. Paul's qualities for an overseer are all character traits.
You do not have to be perfect, because nobody is. But leaders will be judged with greater strictness.

left.text: “And if your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it from you; it is better for you to enter life crippled or lame, than, having two hands or two feet, to be cast into the eternal fire.

right.text: And if your right hand makes you stumble, cut it off and throw it from you; for it is better for you to lose one of the parts of your body, than for your whole body to go into hell.

lines.text: Jesus repeats part of His Sermon on the Mount teaching. The hyperbole works like a fence around the Torah: if sin is a place, He sets a fence between His people and it.
But His fence forces people to deal with what is inside, the heart, where sin starts. So what in the disciples' hearts needs to be cut off? Not their literal hands and feet.

src.text: “Woe to the world because of its stumbling blocks! For it is inevitable that stumbling blocks come; nevertheless, woe to that man through whom the stumbling block comes!

lines.text: When the question sinks in, you realize pride is the great temptation that must be cut off and torn out. Otherwise it will lead to despising the little ones (v10), cause them to stumble (v6), and scatter the sheep.

src.text: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones, for I say to you that their angels in heaven continually see the face of My Father who is in heaven.

lines.text: The Greek word for despise means to look down upon and scorn. The picture is of someone who does not think of another's value or worth, actively insults them, and so causes them to fall away from God's community.
The LSB brackets verse 11, 'For the Son of Man has come to save that which was lost,' which many early manuscripts lack.

src.text: “What do you think? If any man has one hundred sheep, and one of them has gone astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go and search for the one that is straying? And if it turns out that he finds it, truly I say to you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine which have not gone astray.

lines.text: Jesus contrasts despising a person with a shepherd so concerned about losing even one sheep that he leaves the rest to reclaim it.
Luke tells the same parable to grumbling Pharisees and scribes, about one sinner who repents (Luke 15:3-7).

left.text: Those who are sickly you have not strengthened, and the diseased you have not healed, and the broken you have not bound up, and the scattered you have not brought back, nor have you searched for the lost; but with strength and with severity you have dominated them.

right.text: My flock wandered through all the mountains and on every high hill; My flock was scattered over all the surface of the earth, and there was no one to seek or search for them.

lines.text: Jesus does not quote one passage here; He recalls a theme from the Tanakh: shepherding God's people properly. The clearest echo, the video believes, is Ezekiel 34. Read it side by side with Matthew 18.
Israel's leaders had become corrupt and failed in their mission, so God's people were scattered and strayed from their purpose to be His ambassadors to the world. 'Scattered. Scattered. Scattered.'

left.text: For thus says Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I Myself will seek My sheep and care for them.

right.text: “Then I will establish over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will shepherd them; he will shepherd them himself and be their shepherd.

lines.text: The disciples made a mistake, and Jesus brought them back to Ezekiel 34. They are the future leaders of the church; they must not become the shepherds who feed themselves.
Matthew has already shown Jesus' compassion on crowds 'like sheep without a shepherd' (9:36).

TERMS.def: One of five long blocks of Jesus' teaching in Matthew; chapter 18 is the fourth, on community.
Believers who are lowly or vulnerable, not only young children.
Greek skandalon: something that trips a person into sin or out of faith.
Extra boundaries that keep people far from breaking a command (Mishnah Avot 1:1).
A hint back to Scripture; here the shepherd theme of Ezekiel 34.
Lowliness and dependence on God, like a child's on a parent. The captions write 'humilies.'

WORDS.gloss: To turn; here 'be converted,' turn around.
Millstone; with onikos, a donkey-turned millstone. Look up: BDAG, μύλος.
To shepherd, feed a flock; as a noun, shepherd.
To scatter. Look up: BDB or HALOT, פוץ.

BACKGROUND.p: The Mishnah opens with the saying of the Men of the Great Assembly: 'Be patient in [the administration of] justice, raise many disciples and make a fence round the Torah' (Mishnah Avot 1:1). The video uses the idea for Jesus' hyperbole: a boundary set far from sin itself.
Children had little status. Jesus does not praise children for innocence, but holds up their lowliness and dependence, and identifies Himself with them: whoever receives one 'receives Me' (18:5).
In the ancient Near East kings were called shepherds of their people. Ezekiel 34 indicts Israel's kings and leaders and promises that God Himself, through a coming David, will shepherd His flock.

DEBATES.p: Some read young children, others any humble believer, especially new or weak disciples. Verse 6, 'little ones who believe in Me,' points to believers.

Verse 10 is a classic text for guardian angels. Others take it more generally: those who serve the little ones stand in God's presence. Chrysostom reads it of angels who have 'fuller confidence' before God.
The video links the argument to the temple tax (17:24-27). Mark and Luke place it after the second passion prediction, perhaps a rivalry over Peter, James and John going up the mountain.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: On the reread, the video says 'greatest in the kingdom of God'; verse 4 says the kingdom of heaven.
The video reads from another translation. In 18:6 the LSB has 'to stumble' where the video says to sin, and in 5:5 it has 'Blessed are the lowly' where the video says meek.
Verse 5 is about receiving a child; the warning about causing to stumble begins in verse 6.
The link between the temple tax and the disciples' argument is the video's suggestion; Matthew says only 'At that time' (18:1).
The 'fence around the Torah' saying comes from Mishnah Avot 1:1, about the sages' added rules; applying it to Jesus' hyperbole is the video's comparison.
The captions write 'humilies' for humility, 'biatitudes' for Beatitudes, 'rabbitical' for rabbinical, 'shephering' for shepherding and 'hund' for hundred.

QUESTIONS: Why is 'Who then is greatest?' the wrong question?
What does a child's dependence teach you about your own relationship with the Father?
Whose faith could your choices strengthen or weaken this week?
If pride is what must be cut off, what does that look like for you in practice?
Read Ezekiel 34 beside Matthew 18. What does God expect of shepherds?
Who are the 'little ones' around you that are easy to overlook?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson, stated plainly: in order to be a part of God's community, Jesus' disciples must get rid of all forms of pride and self-seeking. They must be tremendously concerned with depending on God and taking care of His sheep. When a person becomes prideful, the quickest way to see it is their lack of concern for those around them. When God blesses a prideful person's ministry, they use it to glorify themselves and forget the sheep. The kingdom is not a game; it is a mission of partnering with God to put the world back together one soul at a time, and pride is one of the great enemies of His shalom. The teacher asks viewers to work out the lesson in their own circles of influence.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): name one 'little one' in your church or family who could be overlooked. This week, do one concrete thing that values them, and pray Psalm 131:1-2 before you do it.

2. Matthew 18:12-14: One sheep straying
   Shepherd Matthew 18:12-13: "“What do you think? If any man has one hundred sheep, and one of them has gone astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go and search for the one that is straying? And if it turns out that he finds it, truly I say to you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine which have not gone astray." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+18:12-13
   (video) Jesus contrasts despising a person with a shepherd so concerned about losing even one sheep that he leaves the rest to reclaim it.
   [Background] Luke tells the same parable to grumbling Pharisees and scribes, about one sinner who repents (Luke 15:3-7). (Luke 15:3-7)
3. Ezekiel 34:2-6: Woe to the shepherds
   Ezekiel (Ezekiel 34:4, LSB): "Those who are sickly you have not strengthened, and the diseased you have not healed, and the broken you have not bound up, and the scattered you have not brought back, nor have you searched for the lost; but with strength and with severity you have dominated them."
   Ezekiel (Ezekiel 34:6, LSB): "My flock wandered through all the mountains and on every high hill; My flock was scattered over all the surface of the earth, and there was no one to seek or search for them."
   (video) Jesus does not quote one passage here; He recalls a theme from the Tanakh: shepherding God's people properly. The clearest echo, the video believes, is Ezekiel 34. Read it side by side with Matthew 18.
   (video) Israel's leaders had become corrupt and failed in their mission, so God's people were scattered and strayed from their purpose to be His ambassadors to the world. 'Scattered. Scattered. Scattered.'
4. Ezekiel 34:11, 23: One shepherd, My servant David
   God (Ezekiel 34:11, LSB): "For thus says Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I Myself will seek My sheep and care for them."
   God (Ezekiel 34:23, LSB): "“Then I will establish over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will shepherd them; he will shepherd them himself and be their shepherd."
   (video) The disciples made a mistake, and Jesus brought them back to Ezekiel 34. They are the future leaders of the church; they must not become the shepherds who feed themselves.
   [Background] Matthew has already shown Jesus' compassion on crowds 'like sheep without a shepherd' (9:36). (Matthew 9:36)

## Key people
- The disciples: Argue about greatness; their question reveals pride. [Background] They will lead the church; Jesus says the great must be servants (20:26).
- The child: A real child, set in the middle as a picture of lowly dependence. [Background] Mark says Jesus took him in His arms (Mark 9:36).
- The little ones: Believers who can be caused to stumble or be despised. [Background] Matthew uses 'little ones' of disciples elsewhere too (10:42).
- The shepherds of Israel: Ezekiel's corrupt leaders who fed themselves and scattered the flock. [Background] God promises to seek His sheep Himself (Ezekiel 34:11).
- Ezekiel: The prophet whose chapter 34 Jesus recalls. [Background] A priest among the exiles in Babylon (Ezekiel 1:3).

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum: Mark places the argument and the child in a house here (Mark 9:33).
- Bethsaida: Peter, Andrew and Philip's town (John 1:44).
- Magdala: A fishing town on the west shore.
- Tiberias: Herod Antipas' capital on the lake.

## Key terms
- Discourse: One of five long blocks of Jesus' teaching in Matthew; chapter 18 is the fourth, on community.
- Little ones: Believers who are lowly or vulnerable, not only young children.
- Stumbling block: Greek skandalon: something that trips a person into sin or out of faith.
- Fence around the Torah: Extra boundaries that keep people far from breaking a command (Mishnah Avot 1:1).
- Remez: A hint back to Scripture; here the shepherd theme of Ezekiel 34.
- Humility: Lowliness and dependence on God, like a child's on a parent. The captions write 'humilies.'

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- A fence around the Torah: The Mishnah opens with the saying of the Men of the Great Assembly: 'Be patient in [the administration of] justice, raise many disciples and make a fence round the Torah' (Mishnah Avot 1:1). The video uses the idea for Jesus' hyperbole: a boundary set far from sin itself.
- Children in the ancient world: Children had little status. Jesus does not praise children for innocence, but holds up their lowliness and dependence, and identifies Himself with them: whoever receives one 'receives Me' (18:5).
- Shepherds as leaders: In the ancient Near East kings were called shepherds of their people. Ezekiel 34 indicts Israel's kings and leaders and promises that God Himself, through a coming David, will shepherd His flock.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]

- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "So exceedingly dear to me is all that is lowly and artless." Homilies on Matthew 58, on 18:5. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Do you see by how many things He is urging to the care of our mean brethren." Homilies on Matthew 59, on 18:10-14. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Who are the 'little ones'? Some read young children, others any humble believer, especially new or weak disciples. Verse 6, 'little ones who believe in Me,' points to believers.
- Their angels Verse 10 is a classic text for guardian angels. Others take it more generally: those who serve the little ones stand in God's presence. Chrysostom reads it of angels who have 'fuller confidence' before God.
- Why did they argue? The video links the argument to the temple tax (17:24-27). Mark and Luke place it after the second passion prediction, perhaps a rivalry over Peter, James and John going up the mountain.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- On the reread, the video says 'greatest in the kingdom of God'; verse 4 says the kingdom of heaven.
- The video reads from another translation. In 18:6 the LSB has 'to stumble' where the video says to sin, and in 5:5 it has 'Blessed are the lowly' where the video says meek.
- Verse 5 is about receiving a child; the warning about causing to stumble begins in verse 6.
- The link between the temple tax and the disciples' argument is the video's suggestion; Matthew says only 'At that time' (18:1).
- The 'fence around the Torah' saying comes from Mishnah Avot 1:1, about the sages' added rules; applying it to Jesus' hyperbole is the video's comparison.
- The captions write 'humilies' for humility, 'biatitudes' for Beatitudes, 'rabbitical' for rabbinical, 'shephering' for shepherding and 'hund' for hundred.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why is 'Who then is greatest?' the wrong question?
2. What does a child's dependence teach you about your own relationship with the Father?
3. Whose faith could your choices strengthen or weaken this week?
4. If pride is what must be cut off, what does that look like for you in practice?
5. Read Ezekiel 34 beside Matthew 18. What does God expect of shepherds?
6. Who are the 'little ones' around you that are easy to overlook?

## Application
- (video) The lesson, stated plainly: in order to be a part of God's community, Jesus' disciples must get rid of all forms of pride and self-seeking. They must be tremendously concerned with depending on God and taking care of His sheep. When a person becomes prideful, the quickest way to see it is their lack of concern for those around them. When God blesses a prideful person's ministry, they use it to glorify themselves and forget the sheep. The kingdom is not a game; it is a mission of partnering with God to put the world back together one soul at a time, and pride is one of the great enemies of His shalom. The teacher asks viewers to work out the lesson in their own circles of influence.
- Study note (added): name one 'little one' in your church or family who could be overlooked. This week, do one concrete thing that values them, and pray Psalm 131:1-2 before you do it.
